_**Tyrannosaurus**_ ([/t ɪ ˌ r æ n ə ˈ s ɔː r ə s,t aɪ-/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"))[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-title-1) is a [genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genus "Genus") of large [theropod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theropoda "Theropoda") dinosaur. The [type species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_species "Type species")_**Tyrannosaurus rex**_ (_rex_ meaning 'king' in [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin")), often shortened to _**T. rex**_ or colloquially **T-Rex**, is one of the best represented theropods. It lived throughout what is now western [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), on what was then an island continent known as [Laramidia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laramidia "Laramidia"). _Tyrannosaurus_ had a much wider range than other [tyrannosaurids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosauridae "Tyrannosauridae"). [Fossils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil "Fossil") are found in a variety of [geological formations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geological_formations "Geological formations") which have been [dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geochronology "Geochronology") to the late [Maastrichtian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastrichtian "Maastrichtian") age of the late [Cretaceous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous "Cretaceous") period, 69 to 66[million years ago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mya_(unit) "Mya (unit)"), with isolated specimens possibly indicating an earlier origin in the middle [Campanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campanian "Campanian") age. It was one of the last known members of the tyrannosaurids and among the last non-[avian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird "Bird") dinosaurs to exist before the [Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous%E2%80%93Paleogene_extinction_event "Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event").

Like other tyrannosaurids, _Tyrannosaurus_ was a [bipedal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biped "Biped") carnivore with a massive skull balanced by a long, heavy tail. Relative to its large and powerful hind limbs, the forelimbs of _Tyrannosaurus_ were short but unusually powerful for their size, and they had two clawed digits. The most complete specimen measures 12.3–12.4 m (40–41 ft) in length, but according to most modern estimates, _Tyrannosaurus_ could have exceeded sizes of 13 m (43 ft) in length, 3.7–4 m (12–13 ft) in hip height, and 8.8 t (8.7 long tons; 9.7 short tons) in mass. Although some other theropods might have rivaled or exceeded _Tyrannosaurus_ in [size](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur_size "Dinosaur size"), it is still among the largest known land predators, with its estimated bite force being the largest among all terrestrial animals. By far the largest carnivore in its environment, _Tyrannosaurus rex_ was most likely an [apex predator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apex_predator "Apex predator"), preying upon [hadrosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrosaur "Hadrosaur"), juvenile armored herbivores like [ceratopsians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceratopsia "Ceratopsia") and [ankylosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankylosaur "Ankylosaur"), and possibly [sauropods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauropod "Sauropod"). The question of whether _Tyrannosaurus_ was an apex predator or a pure scavenger was among the longest debates in [paleontology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleontology "Paleontology"). Most paleontologists today accept that _Tyrannosaurus_ was a predator, and the idea of _Tyrannosaurus_ being primarily a scavenger has been discredited.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-2)

Some [specimens of _Tyrannosaurus rex_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specimens_of_Tyrannosaurus "Specimens of Tyrannosaurus") are nearly complete skeletons. [Soft tissue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_tissue "Soft tissue") and [proteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein "Protein") have been reported in at least one of these specimens. The abundance of fossil material has allowed significant research into many aspects of the animal's biology, including its life history and [biomechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomechanics "Biomechanics"). The feeding habits, [physiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology"), and potential speed of _Tyrannosaurus rex_ are a few subjects of debate. Its [taxonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxonomy_(biology) "Taxonomy (biology)") is also controversial. The Asian _[Tarbosaurus bataar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarbosaurus\_bataar "Tarbosaurus bataar")_ is very closely related to _Tyrannosaurus_ and has sometimes been seen as a species of this genus. Several North American tyrannosaurids have been [synonymized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synonym_(biology) "Synonym (biology)") with _Tyrannosaurus_, while some _Tyrannosaurus_ specimens have been proposed as distinct species. The validity of these species, such as the more recently discovered _**T. mcraeensis**_, is contentious.

_Tyrannosaurus_ has been one of the best-known dinosaurs since the early 20th century. Science writer [Riley Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riley_Black "Riley Black") has called it the "ultimate dinosaur". Its fossils have been a popular attraction in museums and it has appeared in media like _[Jurassic Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurassic\_Park "Jurassic Park")_.

## History of research

See also: [Specimens of _Tyrannosaurus_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specimens_of_Tyrannosaurus "Specimens of Tyrannosaurus")

### Earliest finds

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/AMNH_3982_Manospondylus.jpg/250px-AMNH_3982_Manospondylus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AMNH_3982_Manospondylus.jpg)

[Type specimen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_(biology) "Type (biology)") (AMNH 3982) of _Manospondylus gigas_

A tooth from what is now documented as a _Tyrannosaurus rex_ was found in July 1874 upon [South Table Mountain (Colorado)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Table_Mountain_(Colorado) "South Table Mountain (Colorado)") by [Jarvis Hall (Colorado)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarvis_Hall_(Colorado) "Jarvis Hall (Colorado)") student Peter T. Dotson under the auspices of [Arthur Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Lakes "Arthur Lakes") near [Golden, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden,_Colorado "Golden, Colorado"), in sediments belonging to the [Denver Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Formation "Denver Formation").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-3)_[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite\_note-:02-4)_ In the early 1890s, [John Bell Hatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bell_Hatcher "John Bell Hatcher") collected postcranial elements in eastern [Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming "Wyoming"). The fossils were believed to be from the large species _[Ornithomimus grandis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornithomimus "Ornithomimus")_ (now _[Deinodon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinodon "Deinodon")_) but are now considered _T. rex_ remains.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-quinlanetal2007-5)

In 1892, [Edward Drinker Cope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Drinker_Cope "Edward Drinker Cope") found two vertebral fragments of a large dinosaur. Cope believed the fragments belonged to an "agathaumid" ([ceratopsid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceratopsidae "Ceratopsidae")) dinosaur, and named them _Manospondylus gigas_, meaning "giant porous vertebra", in reference to the numerous openings for blood vessels he found in the bone.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-quinlanetal2007-5) The _M. gigas_ remains were, in 1907, identified by Hatcher as those of a theropod rather than a ceratopsid.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-6)

[Henry Fairfield Osborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Fairfield_Osborn "Henry Fairfield Osborn") recognized the similarity between _Manospondylus gigas_ and _T. rex_ as early as 1917, by which time the second vertebra had been lost. Owing to the fragmentary nature of the _Manospondylus_ vertebrae, Osborn did not synonymize the two genera, instead considering the older genus indeterminate.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-osborn1917-7) In June 2000, the [Black Hills Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute "Black Hills Institute") found around 10% of a _Tyrannosaurus_ skeleton ([BHI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute "Black Hills Institute") 6248) at a site that might have been the original _M. gigas_ locality.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-larson2008-8) While Larson initially considered this specimen as the same animal as the _M. gigas_ holotype and suggested that it would take priority over _T. rex_, other researchers including Christopher Brochu remained skeptical that the name _T. rex_ would be abandoned.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-McTavish2000-9) In 2003, Brochu further argued that although both taxa probably represent the same species, it is impossible to demonstrate that the specimen discovered by the Black Hills Institute represents the same animal as _M. gigas_ due to the poor preservation of the _M. gigas_ holotype; additionally, following the 2000 [International Code of Zoological Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Code_of_Zoological_Nomenclature "International Code of Zoological Nomenclature") amendment, a name in popular usage like _T. rex_ has priority over a name with technical priority but not used as a valid name in formal literature after the year 1899 for over fifty years like _M. gigas_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-11)

### Skeleton discovery and naming

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Tyrannosaurus_skeleton.jpg/250px-Tyrannosaurus_skeleton.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_skeleton.jpg)

Outdated skeletal restoration by [William D. Matthew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Diller_Matthew "William Diller Matthew") from 1905, published alongside Osborn's description paper

[Barnum Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnum_Brown "Barnum Brown"), assistant curator of the [American Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Museum_of_Natural_History "American Museum of Natural History"), found the first partial skeleton of _T. rex_ in eastern Wyoming in 1900. Brown found another partial skeleton in the [Hell Creek Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell_Creek_Formation "Hell Creek Formation") in Montana in 1902, comprising approximately 34 fossilized bones.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-osborn1905-12) Writing at the time Brown said "Quarry No. 1 contains the femur, pubes, humerus, three vertebrae and two undetermined bones of a large Carnivorous Dinosaur not described by [Marsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Othniel_Charles_Marsh "Othniel Charles Marsh").... I have never seen anything like it from the [Cretaceous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous "Cretaceous")."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-dingus2010-13)[Henry Fairfield Osborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Fairfield_Osborn "Henry Fairfield Osborn"), president of the [American Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Museum_of_Natural_History "American Museum of Natural History"), named the second skeleton _T. rex_ in 1905. The generic name is derived from the [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language") words τύραννος (_tyrannos_, meaning "tyrant") and [σαῦρος](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%CF%83%CE%B1%E1%BF%A6%CF%81%CE%BF%CF%82 "wikt:σαῦρος") (_sauros_, meaning "lizard"). Osborn used the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language") word _rex_, meaning "king", for the specific name. The full [binomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_nomenclature "Binomial nomenclature") therefore translates to "tyrant lizard the king" or "King Tyrant Lizard", emphasizing the animal's size and presumed dominance over other species of the time.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-osborn1905-12)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a2/Dynamosaurus_holotype.jpg/250px-Dynamosaurus_holotype.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dynamosaurus_holotype.jpg)

_Dynamosaurus imperiosus_[holotype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holotype "Holotype") (NHMUK PV R8020, previously AMNH 5886) on display at the [Natural History Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_History_Museum,_London "Natural History Museum, London"), London

Osborn named the other specimen _Dynamosaurus imperiosus_ in a paper in 1905.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-osborn1905-12) In 1906, Osborn recognized that the two skeletons were from the same species and selected _Tyrannosaurus_ as the preferred name.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-osborn1906-14) In 1941, the _T. rex_ type specimen was sold to the [Carnegie Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Museum_of_Natural_History "Carnegie Museum of Natural History") in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, for $7,000 (equivalent to $153,224 in 2025).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-dingus2010-13) The original _Dynamosaurus_ material now resides in the collections of the [Natural History Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_History_Museum,_London "Natural History Museum, London"), London.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Breithaupt-15)_Dynamosaurus_ would later be honored by the 2018 description of another species of tyrannosaurid by Andrew McDonald and colleagues, _[Dynamoterror dynastes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamoterror\_dynastes "Dynamoterror dynastes")_, whose name was chosen in reference to the 1905 name, as it had been a "childhood favorite" of McDonald's.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-McDonald2018-16)

From the 1910s through the end of the 1950s, Barnum's discoveries remained the only specimens of _Tyrannosaurus_, as the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") and wars kept many paleontologists out of the field.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-larson2008-8)

### Continued study

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/FMNH_SUE_Trex.jpg/250px-FMNH_SUE_Trex.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FMNH_SUE_Trex.jpg)

Specimen "[Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)")", [Field Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History"), Chicago (with some bones reconstructed)

Beginning in the 1960s, there was renewed interest in _Tyrannosaurus_, resulting in the recovery of 42 skeletons (5–80% complete by bone count) from western North America.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-larson2008-8) In 1967, Dr. William MacMannis located and recovered the skeleton named "MOR 008", which is 15% complete by bone count and has a reconstructed skull displayed at the [Museum of the Rockies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_the_Rockies "Museum of the Rockies"). The 1990s saw numerous discoveries, with nearly twice as many finds as in all previous years, including two of the most complete skeletons found to date: [Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)") and [Stan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_(dinosaur) "Stan (dinosaur)").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-larson2008-8)

[Sue Hendrickson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Hendrickson "Sue Hendrickson"), an [amateur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur "Amateur") paleontologist, discovered the most complete (approximately 85%) and largest _Tyrannosaurus_ skeleton in the [Hell Creek Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell_Creek_Formation "Hell Creek Formation") on August 12, 1990. The specimen Sue, named after the discoverer, was the object of a legal battle over its ownership. In 1997, the litigation was settled in favor of Maurice Williams, the original land owner. The fossil collection was purchased by the [Field Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") at auction for $7.6 million, making it the most expensive dinosaur skeleton until the sale of Stan for $31.8 million in 2020.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-17) From 1998 to 1999, Field Museum of Natural History staff spent over 25,000 hours taking the rock off the bones.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Sueprep-18) The bones were then shipped to [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") where the mount was constructed, then shipped back to Chicago for the final assembly. The mounted skeleton opened to the public on May 17, 2000, in the Field Museum of Natural History. A study of this specimen's fossilized bones showed that Sue reached full size at age 19 and died at the age of 28, the longest estimated life of any tyrannosaur known.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Ericksonetal2004TyrannosaurGigantism-19)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Scotty_Tyrannosaurus.jpg/250px-Scotty_Tyrannosaurus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scotty_Tyrannosaurus.jpg)

Replica of "[Scotty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotty_(dinosaur) "Scotty (dinosaur)")", the largest known specimen, exhibited in Japan

Another _Tyrannosaurus_, nicknamed Stan (NHMAD 2020.00001, formerly BHI 3033[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Boeye2026-20)), in honor of amateur paleontologist Stan Sacrison, was recovered from the Hell Creek Formation in 1992. Stan is the second most complete skeleton found, with 199 bones recovered representing 70% of the total.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-21) This tyrannosaur also had many bone pathologies, including broken and healed ribs, a broken (and healed) neck, and a substantial hole in the back of its head, about the size of a _Tyrannosaurus_ tooth.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-22)

In 1998, 20-year-old Bucky Derflinger noticed a _T. rex_ toe exposed above ground, making him the youngest person to discover a _Tyrannosaurus_. The specimen, dubbed [Bucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specimens_of_Tyrannosaurus#%22Bucky%22:_TCM_2001.90.1 "Specimens of Tyrannosaurus") in honor of its discoverer, was a young adult, 3.0 metres (10 ft) tall and 11 metres (35 ft) long. Bucky is the first _Tyrannosaurus_ to be found that preserved a [furcula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Furcula "Furcula") (wishbone). Bucky is permanently displayed at [The Children's Museum of Indianapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Children's_Museum_of_Indianapolis "The Children's Museum of Indianapolis").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-23)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Tyrannosaurus_specimens.svg/250px-Tyrannosaurus_specimens.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_specimens.svg)

The specimens "Sue", AMNH 5027, "Stan", and "Jane", to scale with a human.

In the summer of 2000, crews organized by [Jack Horner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Horner_(paleontologist) "Jack Horner (paleontologist)") discovered five _Tyrannosaurus_ skeletons near the [Fort Peck Reservoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Peck_Reservoir "Fort Peck Reservoir").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-bbc-horner-24) In 2001, a 50% complete skeleton of a juvenile _Tyrannosaurus_ was discovered in the Hell Creek Formation by a crew from the [Burpee Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burpee_Museum_of_Natural_History "Burpee Museum of Natural History"). Dubbed Jane (BMRP 2002.4.1), the find was thought to be the first known skeleton of a [pygmy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pygmy "Pygmy") tyrannosaurid, _[Nanotyrannus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanotyrannus "Nanotyrannus")_, but other researchers considered it as the most complete juvenile _T. rex_;[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-currieetal2003-25) currently exhibited at the Burpee Museum of Natural History, Jane is now re-described as the holotype of _N. lethaeus_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Z&N25-26) In 2002, a skeleton nicknamed "Wyrex", discovered by amateur collectors Dan Wells and Don Wyrick, had 114 bones and was 38% complete. The dig was concluded over 3 weeks in 2004 by the [Black Hills Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hills_Institute "Black Hills Institute") with the first live [online](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online "Online")_Tyrannosaurus_ excavation providing daily reports, photos, and video.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-larson2008-8)

In 2006, [Montana State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana_State_University "Montana State University") revealed that it possessed the largest _Tyrannosaurus_ skull yet discovered (from a specimen named MOR 008), measuring 5 feet (152 cm) long.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-MOR008-27) Subsequent comparisons indicated that the longest head was 136.5 centimetres (53.7 in) (from specimen LACM 23844) and the widest head was 90.2 centimetres (35.5 in) (from Sue).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-gignac-28)

## Description

### Size

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Longest_theropods.svg/500px-Longest_theropods.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Longest_theropods.svg)

Size (in blue) compared to select giant theropods and a human

_T. rex_ was one of the largest land carnivores of all time. One of its largest and the most complete specimens, nicknamed [Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)") (FMNH PR2081), is located at the [Field Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") in Chicago. Sue measured 12.3–12.8 m (40–42 ft) long,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-SueFMNH-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Hutchinsonet.al.2011-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Holtz2008-31) was 3.66–3.96 m (12.0–13.0 ft) tall at the hips,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-SueFMNH-29)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Sue-32)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-FMNH-33) and according to the most recent studies, using a variety of techniques, maximum body masses have been estimated approximately 8.4–9.22 t (8.27–9.07 long tons; 9.26–10.16 short tons).[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Persons-34)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-HartmanMassEstimate-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-nicolas2014-36) A specimen nicknamed [Scotty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotty_(dinosaur) "Scotty (dinosaur)") (RSM P2523.8), located at the [Royal Saskatchewan Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Saskatchewan_Museum "Royal Saskatchewan Museum"), is reported to measure 13 m (43 ft) in length. Using a mass estimation technique that extrapolates from the [circumference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circumference "Circumference") of the femur, Scotty was estimated as the largest known specimen at 8.87 t (8.73 long tons; 9.78 short tons) in body mass.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Persons-34)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Lyle2019-37)

Not every adult _Tyrannosaurus_ specimen recovered is as big. Historically average adult mass estimates have varied widely over the years, from as low as 4.5 t (4.4 long tons; 5.0 short tons),[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-andersonetal1985-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-bakker1986-39) to more than 7.2 t (7.1 long tons; 7.9 short tons),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-henderson1999-40) with most modern estimates ranging between 5.4 and 8.0 t (5.3 and 7.9 long tons; 6.0 and 8.8 short tons).[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Hutchinsonet.al.2011-30)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-ericksonetal2004-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-farlowetal1995-42)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-seebacher2001-43)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-christiansenfarina2004-44)

A 2024 study found that there was little evidence of size-based sexual dimorphism in _T. rex_.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Mallon&Hone24-45)

### Skull

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Tyrannosaurus_rex_AMNH_5027_skull.png/250px-Tyrannosaurus_rex_AMNH_5027_skull.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_rex_AMNH_5027_skull.png)

Skull of specimen AMNH 5027 with labelled diagrams in dorsal, lateral, anterior, posterior, and medial (lower jaw) views

The largest known _T. rex_ skulls measure up to 1.52 m (5 ft 0 in) in length.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-MOR008-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-SueFMNH-29) Large [fenestrae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenestra_(anatomy) "Fenestra (anatomy)") (openings) in the skull reduced weight, as in all carnivorous theropods. In other respects _Tyrannosaurus_'s skull was significantly different from those of large non-[tyrannosaurid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurid "Tyrannosaurid") theropods. It was extremely wide at the rear but had a narrow snout, allowing unusually good [binocular vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binocular_vision "Binocular vision").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Stevens2006Binocular-46)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-jaffe-47) The skull bones were massive and the [nasals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_bone "Nasal bone") and some other bones were fused, preventing movement between them; but many were [pneumatized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumatized_bones "Pneumatized bones") (contained a "honeycomb" of tiny air spaces) and thus lighter. These and other skull-strengthening features are part of the [tyrannosaurid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurid "Tyrannosaurid") trend towards an increasingly powerful bite, which easily surpassed that of all non-tyrannosaurids.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-SnivelyHendersonPhillips2006FusedVaultedNasals-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-MM03-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-GEetal96-50) The tip of the upper jaw was U-shaped (most non-tyrannosauroid carnivores had V-shaped upper jaws), which increased the amount of tissue and bone a tyrannosaur could rip out with one bite, although it also increased the stresses on the front teeth.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-holtz1994-51)

The teeth of _T. rex_ displayed marked [heterodonty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterodont "Heterodont") (differences in shape).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Smith2005HeterodontyTRex-52) The [premaxillary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premaxilla "Premaxilla") teeth, four per side at the front of the upper jaw, were closely packed, _D_-shaped in cross-section, had reinforcing ridges on the rear surface, were [incisiform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incisor "Incisor") (their tips were chisel-like blades) and curved backwards. The _D_-shaped cross-section, reinforcing ridges and backwards curve reduced the risk that the teeth would snap when _Tyrannosaurus_ bit and pulled. The remaining teeth were robust, like "lethal bananas" rather than daggers, more widely spaced and also had reinforcing ridges.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-New_Scientist1998DinosaurDetectives-53) Those in the upper jaw, twelve per side in mature individuals,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10) were larger than their counterparts of the lower jaw, except at the rear. The largest found so far is estimated to have been 30.5 cm (12.0 in) long including the root when the animal was alive, making it the largest tooth of any carnivorous dinosaur yet found.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-SueFMNH2-54) The lower jaw was robust. Its front [dentary bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dentary_bone "Dentary bone") bore thirteen teeth. Behind the tooth row, the lower jaw became notably taller.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10) The upper and lower jaws of _Tyrannosaurus_, like those of many dinosaurs, possessed numerous [foramina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foramen "Foramen"), or small holes in the bone. Various functions have been proposed for these foramina, such as a crocodile-like sensory system[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carr2017-55) or evidence of [extra-oral structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integument "Integument") such as scales or potentially lips,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-56)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-:0-57)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-MontevialeCroc-58) with subsequent research on theropod tooth wear patterns supporting such a proposition.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-CullenEtAl23-59)

### Skeleton

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Tyrannosaurus-rex-Profile-steveoc86_%28coloured%29%28mirror%29.png/250px-Tyrannosaurus-rex-Profile-steveoc86_%28coloured%29%28mirror%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus-rex-Profile-steveoc86_(coloured)(mirror).png)

[Life restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleoart "Paleoart") showing scaly skin with sparse feathering, and lipped jaws

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7f/Tyrannosaurus_Sue_skeletal_reconstruction.png/250px-Tyrannosaurus_Sue_skeletal_reconstruction.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_Sue_skeletal_reconstruction.png)

Skeletal reconstruction of specimen "Sue"

The [vertebral column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebral_column "Vertebral column") of _Tyrannosaurus_ consisted of ten neck vertebrae, thirteen back vertebrae and five sacral vertebrae. The number of tail vertebrae is unknown and could well have varied between individuals but probably numbered at least forty. Sue was mounted with forty-seven of such caudal vertebrae.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10) The neck of _T. rex_ formed a natural S-shaped curve like that of other theropods. Compared to these, it was exceptionally short, deep and muscular to support the massive head. The second vertebra, the axis, was especially short. The remaining neck vertebrae were weakly opisthocoelous, i.e. with a convex front of the vertebral body and a concave rear. The vertebral bodies had single pleurocoels, pneumatic depressions created by [air sacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_sac "Air sac"), on their sides.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10) The vertebral bodies of the torso were robust but with a narrow waist. Their undersides were keeled. The front sides were concave with a deep vertical trough. They had large pleurocoels. Their neural spines had very rough front and rear sides for the attachment of strong tendons. The sacral vertebrae were fused to each other, both in their vertebral bodies and neural spines. They were pneumatized. They were connected to the pelvis by transverse processes and sacral ribs. The tail was heavy and moderately long, in order to balance the massive head and torso and to provide space for massive [locomotor muscles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_locomotion "Animal locomotion") that attached to the thighbones. The thirteenth tail vertebra formed the transition point between the deep tail base and the middle tail that was stiffened by a rather long front articulation processes. The underside of the trunk was covered by eighteen or nineteen pairs of segmented belly ribs.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/The_Right_Arm_of_SUE.jpg/250px-The_Right_Arm_of_SUE.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Right_Arm_of_SUE.jpg)

Right forelimb of specimen "Sue"

The [shoulder girdle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoulder_girdle "Shoulder girdle") was longer than the entire forelimb. The shoulder blade had a narrow shaft but was exceptionally expanded at its upper end. It connected via a long forward protrusion to the [coracoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coracoid "Coracoid"), which was rounded. Both shoulder blades were connected by a small [furcula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Furcula "Furcula"). The paired breast bones possibly were made of [cartilage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartilage "Cartilage") only.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)

The forelimb or arm was very short. The upper arm bone, the humerus, was short but robust. It had a narrow upper end with an exceptionally rounded head. The lower arm bones, the [ulna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulna "Ulna") and radius, were straight elements, much shorter than the humerus. The second [metacarpal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacarpus "Metacarpus") was longer and wider than the first, whereas normally in theropods the opposite is true. The forelimbs had only two clawed fingers,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10) along with an additional splint-like small third [metacarpal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacarpus "Metacarpus") representing the remnant of a third digit.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-CLKC08-60)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6d/UCMP_Trex_pelvis_2.JPG/250px-UCMP_Trex_pelvis_2.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UCMP_Trex_pelvis_2.JPG)

Pelvic girdle of specimen MOR 555

The [pelvis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelvis "Pelvis") was a large structure. Its upper bone, the [ilium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilium_(bone) "Ilium (bone)"), was both very long and high, providing an extensive attachment area for hindlimb muscles. The front [pubic bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pubic_bone "Pubic bone") ended in an enormous pubic boot, longer than the entire shaft of the element. The rear [ischium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ischium "Ischium") was slender and straight, pointing obliquely to behind and below.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)

In contrast to the arms, the hindlimbs were among the longest in proportion to body size of any theropod. In the foot, the [metatarsus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metatarsus "Metatarsus") was "arctometatarsalian", meaning that the part of the third metatarsal near the ankle was pinched. The third metatarsal was also exceptionally sinuous.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10) Compensating for the immense bulk of the animal, many bones throughout the skeleton were hollowed, reducing its weight without significant loss of strength.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-brochu2003-10)

## Classification

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/Tyrannosaurus_skulls_Japan.jpg/250px-Tyrannosaurus_skulls_Japan.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_skulls_Japan.jpg)

Skull casts of different _Tyrannosaurus_ specimens

_Tyrannosaurus_ is the [type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_(biology) "Type (biology)") genus of the superfamily [Tyrannosauroidea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosauroidea "Tyrannosauroidea"), the [family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_(taxonomy) "Family (taxonomy)")[Tyrannosauridae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosauridae "Tyrannosauridae"), and the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae; in other words it is the standard by which paleontologists decide whether to include other species in the same group. Other members of the tyrannosaurine subfamily include the North American _[Daspletosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daspletosaurus "Daspletosaurus")_ and the Asian _[Tarbosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarbosaurus "Tarbosaurus")_,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-currieetal2003-25)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-holtz2004-61) both of which have occasionally been synonymized with _Tyrannosaurus_.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-paul1988-62)

Tyrannosaurids were once commonly thought to be descendants of earlier large theropods such as [megalosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinosauroidea "Spinosauroidea") and [carnosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnosauria "Carnosauria"), although more recently they were reclassified with the generally smaller [coelurosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coelurosauria "Coelurosauria").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-holtz1994-51) The earliest tyrannosaur group were the crested proceratosaurids, while later and more derived members belong to the [Pantyrannosauria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantyrannosauria "Pantyrannosauria"). Tyrannosaurs started out as small theropods; however at least some became larger by the [Early Cretaceous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Cretaceous "Early Cretaceous"). It is quite likely that tyrannosauroids rose to prominence after the decline in allosauroid and megalosauroid diversity seen during the early stages of the Late Cretaceous.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-63)

Tyrannosauroids are characterized by their fused nasals and dental arrangement. Pantyrannosaurs are characterized by unique features in their hips as well as an enlarged foramen in the quadrate, a broad postorbital and hourglass shaped nasals. Some of the more derived pantyrannosaurs lack nasal pneumaticity and have a lower humerus to femur ratio with their arms starting to see some reduction. Some pantyrannosaurs started developing an arctometatarsus. Eutyrannosaurs have a rough texture on their nasal bones and their mandibular fenestra is reduced externally. Tyrannosaurids lack kinetic skulls or special crests on their nasal bones, and have a lacrimal with a distinctive process on it. Tyrannosaurids also have an interfenestral strut that is less than half as big as the maxillary fenestra.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-64)

Many [phylogenetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phylogeny "Phylogeny") analyses have found _[Tarbosaurus bataar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarbosaurus\_bataar "Tarbosaurus bataar")_ to be the [sister taxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sister_taxon "Sister taxon") of _T. rex_.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-holtz2004-61) The discovery of the tyrannosaurid _[Lythronax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lythronax "Lythronax")_ further indicates that _Tarbosaurus_ and _Tyrannosaurus_ are closely related, forming a clade with fellow Asian tyrannosaurid _[Zhuchengtyrannus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhuchengtyrannus "Zhuchengtyrannus")_, with _Lythronax_ being their sister taxon.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Loewen13-65)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-66) A further study from 2016 by Steve Brusatte, Thomas Carr and colleagues, also indicates that _Tyrannosaurus_ may have been an immigrant from Asia, as well as a possible descendant of _Tarbosaurus_.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-67)

### Additional species

[![Image 42](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Tarbosaurus_and_Tyrannosaurus.jpg/250px-Tarbosaurus_and_Tyrannosaurus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tarbosaurus_and_Tyrannosaurus.jpg)

Diagram showing the differences between a generalized _Tarbosaurus_ (A) and _Tyrannosaurus rex_ (B) skull

In 1955, Soviet [paleontologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleontology "Paleontology")[Evgeny Maleev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evgeny_Maleev "Evgeny Maleev") named a new species, _Tyrannosaurus bataar_, from [Mongolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolia "Mongolia").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-maleev1955-70) By 1965, this species was renamed as a distinct genus, _Tarbosaurus bataar_.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-rozhdestvensky1965-71) While most paleontologists continue to maintain the two as distinct genera, some authors such as [Thomas Holtz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Holtz "Thomas Holtz"), [Kenneth Carpenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Carpenter "Kenneth Carpenter"), and [Thomas Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Carr_(paleontologist) "Thomas Carr (paleontologist)") argue that the two species are similar enough to be considered members of the same genus, restoring the Mongolian [taxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxon "Taxon")'s original [binomial name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_nomenclature "Binomial nomenclature").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-holtz1994-51)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carpenter1992-72)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carr2017-55)

Some specimens from the Late Cretaceous deposits of [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") have been described as new species of _Tyrannosaurus_: _T._ "lanpingensis" based on isolated [lateral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lateral_(anatomy) "Lateral (anatomy)") tooth from the red beds of [Yunnan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yunnan "Yunnan") in 1975; _T._ "turpanensis" from the [Subashi Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subashi_Formation "Subashi Formation"), [Turpan Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turpan_Basin "Turpan Basin"), [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang") in 1978; and _T. luanchuanensis_ from the [Quiba Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiba_Formation "Quiba Formation"), [Tantou Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tantou_Basin?action=edit&redlink=1 "Tantou Basin (page does not exist)"), [Henan Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henan_Province "Henan Province") in 1979–1980.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-73)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Feng2016-74)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Lucas2018-75) The former two taxa were published without detailed descriptions and are therefore nomina nuda. _T._ "turpanensis" and _T. luanchuanensis_ were tentatively listed as [junior synonyms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synonym_(taxonomy) "Synonym (taxonomy)") of _Tarbosaurus bataar_ by Holtz in 2004; Holtz also listed _T._ "lanpingensis," but as a nomen dubium.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-holtz2004-61)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Feng2016-74)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Lucas2018-75)

VGI, no. 231/3, a large [phalanx bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phalanx_bone "Phalanx bone"), assigned to _Tyrannosaurus_ sp. by Yarkov in 2000, was found in the Lower Maastrichtian of [Bereslavka, Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bereslavka,_Russia "Bereslavka, Russia"). In 2004, Averianov and Yarkov reinterpreted it as a [metacarpal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacarpal "Metacarpal") I or [metatarsal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metatarsal "Metatarsal") I that possibly belongs to [ceratosaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceratosaur "Ceratosaur").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-76) In their 2023 overview, Averianov and Lopatin mention this specimen as well as a single tooth from the same site only as Theropoda indet.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-77)

In 2001, various tyrannosaurid teeth and a metatarsal unearthed in a quarry near [Zhucheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhucheng "Zhucheng"), China, were assigned by Chinese paleontologist [Hu Chengzhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hu_Chengzhi "Hu Chengzhi") to the newly erected species _Tyrannosaurus zhuchengensis_. However, in a nearby site, a right maxilla and left jawbone were assigned to the newly erected tyrannosaurid genus _Zhuchengtyrannus_ in 2011. It is possible that _T. zhuchengensis_ is [synonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synonym_(taxonomy) "Synonym (taxonomy)") with _Zhuchengtyrannus_. In any case, _T. zhuchengensis_ is considered to be a _[nomen dubium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomen\_dubium "Nomen dubium")_ as the holotype lacks [diagnostic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagnosis_(taxonomy) "Diagnosis (taxonomy)") features below the level Tyrannosaurinae.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-78)

In 2006, a fragmentary tyrannosaurid lacrimal (CM 9401) from the [Judith River Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_River_Formation "Judith River Formation") of Fergus County, Montana, was described as?_Tyrannosaurus_ sp. This isolated right lacrimal was originally collected alongside the holotype specimen of _Deinosuchus rugosus_, a giant crocodilian, and remained undescribed until its re-identification as belonging to a tyrannosaurid theropod in the 1980s by paleontologist [Dale Russell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dale_Russell "Dale Russell"). The lacrimal closely resembles those of _Tyrannosaurus rex_ in both size and morphology. Notably, it lacks the "lacrimal horn" typically present in earlier tyrannosaurids like _[Albertosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albertosaurus "Albertosaurus")_ and _[Gorgosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorgosaurus "Gorgosaurus")_, instead exhibiting a distinct rugosity along the dorsal surface—consistent with _T. rex_ and its Asian relative _Tarbosaurus_. The specimen's considerable size places it within the range of known _T. rex_ individuals, suggesting the presence of large tyrannosaurids during the Campanian stage (~75 million years ago), a temporal range earlier than the established Maastrichtian age (~68–66 Ma) for _Tyrannosaurus rex_. However, the exact age and provenance of CM 9401 remain uncertain due to a lack of detailed field documentation.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-79)

In 2018, a paper describing tyrannosaurid teeth from the Two Medicine Formation noted a premaxillary tooth (YPM VPPU 023469) had a strong resemblance to the teeth of [Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(Tyrannosaurus) "Sue (Tyrannosaurus)") to the exclusion of any Campanian tyrannosaurid. Additionally, the authors of this paper suggested that CM 9401 also comes from the Two Medicine Formation, as there were preservational similarities between its locality and the Willow Creek anticline, which is where the tooth was found.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-80) Notably, this would place both specimens in the Flag Butte Member of the Two Medicine Formation, which dates from 77 to 76.3 Ma, far older than any other _Tyrannosaurus_ specimen, and directly contemporaneous with _Daspletosaurus._ In 2025, these specimens, with their old geologic age, were used as evidence by Charlie Scherer to suggest that the Tyrannosaurini did not evolve directly from _Daspletosaurus_.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Scherer2025-81)

### _Tyrannosaurus imperator_ and _Tyrannosaurus regina_

In a 2022 study, [Gregory S. Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_S._Paul "Gregory S. Paul") and colleagues argued that _Tyrannosaurus rex_, as traditionally understood, actually represents three species: the type species _Tyrannosaurus rex_, and two previously unrecognized species: _T. imperator_ (meaning "tyrant lizard emperor") and _T. regina_ (meaning "tyrant lizard queen"). The holotype of the former (_T. imperator_) is the [Sue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_(dinosaur) "Sue (dinosaur)") specimen, and the holotype of the latter (_T. regina_) is [Wankel rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wankel_rex "Wankel rex"). The division into multiple species was primarily based on the high degree of variation in the proportions and robusticity of the [femur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femur "Femur") (and other skeletal elements) across _T. rex_ specimens. Presumed robust and gracile morphotypes and the number of small incisiform teeth in the dentary were also used as a line of evidence. Paul and colleagues categorized the species as follows: _T. rex_ demonstrates robust anatomy, a moderate ratio of femur length vs circumference, and the possession of a singular slender incisiform dentary tooth, _T. imperator_ is robust with a small femur length to circumference ratio and two of the slender teeth, and _T. regina_ is more gracile with a high femur ratio and one of the slender teeth.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-paul2022-82)

However, several leading paleontologists, including [Stephen Brusatte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Brusatte "Stephen Brusatte"), [Thomas Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Carr_(paleontologist) "Thomas Carr (paleontologist)"), [Thomas Holtz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Holtz "Thomas Holtz"), David Hone, [Jingmai O'Connor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingmai_O'Connor "Jingmai O'Connor"), and [Lindsay Zanno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindsay_Zanno "Lindsay Zanno"), criticized the study or expressed skepticism of its conclusions when approached by various media outlets for comment.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-newyorktimes-83)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-84)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-85) Their criticism was subsequently published in a technical paper.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Carr_et.al.(2022)-86) Holtz and Zanno both remarked that it was plausible that more than one species of _Tyrannosaurus_ existed, but felt the new study was insufficient to support the species it proposed. Holtz remarked that, even if _Tyrannosaurus imperator_ represented a distinct species from _Tyrannosaurus rex_, it may represent the same species as _Nanotyrannus lancensis_ and would need to be called _Tyrannosaurus lancensis_. O'Connor, a curator at the Field Museum, where the _T. imperator_ holotype Sue is displayed, regarded the new species as too poorly-supported to justify modifying the exhibit signs. Brusatte, Carr, and O'Connor viewed the distinguishing features proposed between the species as reflecting natural variation within a species. Both Carr and O'Connor expressed concerns about the study's inability to determine which of the proposed species several well-preserved specimens belonged to. Another paleontologist, [Philip J. Currie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_J._Currie "Philip J. Currie"), originally co-authored the study but withdrew from it as he did not want to be involved in naming the new species.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-newyorktimes-83)

In a subsequent paper published in 2025, Paul maintained the validity of _T. imperator_ and _T. regina_, arguing that these proposed species could be further distinguished by the shape of their postorbital bosses (bony rugosities behind the eyes).[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Paul2025-87)

### _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_

[![Image 43](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis_%28skull_reconstruction%29.png/250px-Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis_%28skull_reconstruction%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis_(skull_reconstruction).png)

[![Image 44](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis.png/250px-Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis.png)

Reconstructed skull (top) and speculative [life restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_restoration "Life restoration") (bottom) of _T. mcraeensis_

In 2024, Dalman and colleagues [described](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species_description "Species description") the remains of a tyrannosaur discovered in 1983 in the Campanian-early Maastrichtian [Hall Lake Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hall_Lake_Formation "Hall Lake Formation") in New Mexico. Reposited at the [New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico_Museum_of_Natural_History_and_Science "New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science"), the fossil material (NMMNH P-3698) consists of the right [postorbital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postorbital "Postorbital"), right [squamosal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squamosal "Squamosal"), left [palatine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palatine "Palatine"), and an incomplete [maxilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxilla "Maxilla") from the skull, the left [dentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dentary "Dentary"), right [splenial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splenial "Splenial"), right prearticular, right [angular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_bone "Angular bone") and right [articular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Articular "Articular") from the lower jaws, isolated teeth, and [chevrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haemal_arch "Haemal arch").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-T.mcraeensis-68) Some of the bones were briefly mentioned in 1984 as belonging to _T. rex_,[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Lozinsky1984-88) and described in 1986.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Gillette1986-89)

Lehman and Carpenter (1990) suggested that NMMNH P-3698 belonged to a new tyrannosaurid genus,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-90) while Carr and Williamson (2000) disagreed with their claim.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-91) Sullivan and Lucas (2015) argued that there is little evidence to support NMMNH P-3698 as a specimen of _Tyrannosaurus rex_, so they tentatively classified it as cf. _Tyrannosaurus_ sp.; they also considered that the McRae tyrannosaur lived before the [Lancian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancian "Lancian") (before 67 million years ago) based on its probable association with the _[Alamosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alamosaurus "Alamosaurus")_ fossil.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-92)

[![Image 45](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis_%28mandibular_elements%29.png/250px-Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis_%28mandibular_elements%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_mcraeensis_(mandibular_elements).png)

Mandibular elements of the _T. mcraeensis_ holotype

Dalman et al. (2024) proposed the new name _Tyrannosaurus mcraeensis_ for the holotype (NMMNH P-3698), referencing the McRae Group, the rock layers to which the Hall Lake Formation belongs. The holotype of _T. mcraeensis_ is found in the strata that are around a few million years older than the accepted range of _T. rex_, which existed at the end of the Maastrichtian. The rock layers were initially estimated to date to between 72.7 and 70.9 Ma, correlating to the latest Campanian or earliest Maastrichtian.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-T.mcraeensis-68) However, in a 2024 conference [abstract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstract_(summary) "Abstract (summary)"), the specific stratigraphic layer which yielded _T. mcraeensis_ was estimated to be younger than 69.0 ± 0.4 Ma and older than 66.0 Ma based on the sandstone from the same fossil locality,[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-93) which would suggest that the age of _T. mcraeensis_ is much closer to _T. rex_ than previously thought.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Scherer2025-81)_T. mcraeensis_ was estimated at 12 metres (39 ft) long, which is similar to the size of an adult _T. rex_. The two are distinguished by characters of the skull. Amongst these, the dentary of _T. mcraeensis_ is proportionately longer and possesses a less prominent chin, and the lower jaw shallower than that of _T. rex_, suggesting a weaker bite. The teeth are likewise blunter and more laterally compressed, while the post orbital crests are less prominent. Likewise, the skeletal anatomy showcases shared characteristics with _Tarbosaurus_ and _Zhuchengtyrannus_.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-T.mcraeensis-68)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-NYT-20240111-94)

The validity of _T. mcraeensis_ was subsequently questioned by other researchers in 2025. Morrison and colleagues noted the uncertainty in the previous age estimate of _T. mcraeensis_. The authors argued that the inclusion of the titanosaurian fossil (cf. _Alamosaurus_) as a biostratigraphic marker of the Hall Lake Formation fauna makes the dating problematic due to the fossil having a huge variability in assumed sedimentation rates. The study also suggested the uncertainty in the morphology of _T. mcraeensis_ holotype being reliably outside the known variation of _T. rex_. Regardless of the age and validity of _T. mcraeensis_, the authors concluded that the genus _Tyrannosaurus_ still most likely originated from Laramidia and that the ancestors of this genus possibly migrated from Asia.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-95) Later that year, Voris and colleagues regarded _T. mcraeensis_ as a [junior synonym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junior_synonym "Junior synonym") of _T. rex_, agreeing with the problematic stratigraphic data and finding all of the proposed diagnostic characters of _T. mcraeensis_ to be in the known _T. rex_ specimen range of variation.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-voris25-96) In his study of the _T. rex_ holotype skull, Carr also did not regard _T. mcraeensis_ as a valid species, agreeing with the proposed characters of the _T. mcraeensis_ holotype being visible throughout the hypodigm of _T. rex_.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-97)

### _Nanotyrannus_

Main article: [Nanotyrannus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanotyrannus "Nanotyrannus")

[![Image 46](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Nanotyrannus_lancensis_skull.jpg/250px-Nanotyrannus_lancensis_skull.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nanotyrannus_lancensis_skull.jpg)

Cast of CMNH 7541, the [holotype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holotype "Holotype") of _Nanotyrannus lancensis_, sometimes interpreted as a juvenile _Tyrannosaurus_.

Other tyrannosaur fossils found in the same formations as _T. rex_ were originally classified as separate taxa, including _Aublysodon_ and _Albertosaurus megagracilis_,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-paul1988-62) the latter being named _Dinotyrannus megagracilis_ in 1995.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Olshevsky1995-98) These fossils are now universally considered to belong to juvenile _T. rex_.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carrwilliamson2004-99) A small but nearly complete skull from Montana, 57.2 centimeters (1.88 ft) long, is an exception. This skull, [CMNH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Museum_of_Natural_History "Cleveland Museum of Natural History") 7541, was originally classified as a species of _[Gorgosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorgosaurus "Gorgosaurus")_ (_G. lancensis_) by [Charles W. Gilmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_W._Gilmore "Charles W. Gilmore") in 1946.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-gilmore1946-100) In 1988, the specimen was re-described by [Robert T. Bakker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_T._Bakker "Robert T. Bakker"), Michael Williams, then the curator of paleontology at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History, and [Phil Currie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_J._Currie "Philip J. Currie"), where the original specimen was housed and is now on display. Their initial research indicated that the skull bones were fused, and that it therefore represented an adult specimen. In light of this, Bakker and colleagues assigned the skull to a new genus named _Nanotyrannus_ (meaning "dwarf tyrant", for its apparently small adult size).[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-bakkeretal1988-101) However, in 1999, a detailed analysis by [Thomas Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Carr_(paleontologist) "Thomas Carr (paleontologist)") revealed the specimen to be a juvenile, leading Carr and many other paleontologists to consider it a juvenile _T. rex_ individual.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-carr1999-102)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-juvenilebataar-103)

[![Image 47](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Tyrannosaurus_Rex_Jane.jpg/250px-Tyrannosaurus_Rex_Jane.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tyrannosaurus_Rex_Jane.jpg)

Reconstructed skeleton of "Jane", [Burpee Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burpee_Museum_of_Natural_History "Burpee Museum of Natural History")

In 2001, a more complete juvenile tyrannosaur (nicknamed "Jane", [accession number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accession_number_(cultural_property) "Accession number (cultural property)") BMRP 2002.4.1), suggested to belong to the same species as the original _Nanotyrannus_ specimen, was uncovered. This discovery prompted a conference on tyrannosaurs focused on the issues of the validity of _Nanotyrannus_, held at the [Burpee Museum of Natural History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burpee_Museum_of_Natural_History "Burpee Museum of Natural History") in 2005. Several paleontologists who had previously published opinions that _N. lancensis_ was a valid species, including Currie and Williams, saw the discovery of "Jane" as a confirmation that _Nanotyrannus_ was, in fact, a juvenile _T. rex_.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-currie2003a-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-currieetal2005-105)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-henderson2005-106)[Peter Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Larson "Peter Larson") continued to support the hypothesis that _Nanotyrannus lancensis_ was a separate but closely related species, and also argued that _[Stygivenator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stygivenator "Stygivenator")_ (LACM 28471), which is generally considered to be a juvenile of _Tyrannosaurus rex_, could be a younger specimen of _Nanotyrannus_.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-larson13-107)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-108)

In late 2011, news reports about a 2006 discovery of a new, virtually complete theropod specimen found alongside a [ceratopsid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceratopsid "Ceratopsid") were made. The specimens were studied by Robert Bakker and Peter Larson on-site, who identified the ceratopsian as _[Triceratops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triceratops "Triceratops")_ and the theropod as _Nanotyrannus_.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Nano_Smithsonian_2011-109) It was impossible to determine whether the theropod specimen, nicknamed "Bloody Mary", was distinct from _T. rex_, as the specimen remained in private hands until 2020, when the ownership of the specimen was decided by the [Montana Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana_Supreme_Court "Montana Supreme Court") to be given to the landowners Mary Anne and Lige Murray, who agreed to sell the paired fossils to a U.S.-based museum.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-110) The fossil was acquired by the [North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_Museum_of_Natural_Sciences "North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences") in 2020, after which the museum built an additional research lab space in which to [prepare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil_preparation "Fossil preparation"), study, and display the specimens.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-111)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-112) In 2025, paleontologists [Lindsay Zanno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindsay_Zanno "Lindsay Zanno") and James Napoli published an initial description of the "Bloody Mary" specimen as part of an extensive revision of the genus _Nanotyrannus_. They identified this specimen as a skeletally mature individual of _Nanotyrannus_ and provided several lines of evidence supporting the validity of this genus. They also described a second species, _N. lethaeus_, based on the Jane specimen due to notable differences between it and _N. lancensis_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-Z&N25-26)

## Paleobiology

### Life history

[![Image 48](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Juvenile_Tyrannosaurus_skull_LACM.jpg/250px-Juvenile_Tyrannosaurus_skull_LACM.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Juvenile_Tyrannosaurus_skull_LACM.jpg)

Skull of a juvenile _T. rex_ formerly classified as _Dinotyrannus megagracilis_

The identification of several specimens as juvenile _T. rex_ has allowed scientists to document [ontogenetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontogeny "Ontogeny") changes in the species, estimate the lifespan, and determine how quickly the animals would have grown. The _Stygivenator_ holotype ([LACM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_County_Museum_of_Natural_History "Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History") 28471, the "Jordan theropod"), possibly a juvenile _T. rex_, is estimated to have weighed only 30 kg (66 lb), while the largest adults, such as [FMNH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_Museum_of_Natural_History "Field Museum of Natural History") PR2081 (Sue) most likely weighed about 5,650 kg (12,460 lb). [Histologic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histology "Histology") analysis of _T. rex_ bones showed LACM 28471 had aged only 2 years when it died. Sue was initially estimated at 28 years old, an age which was at the time considered close to the maximum for the species,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-ericksonetal2004-41) but the most recent studies estimate Sue's age at 27–33 years.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-113) Similarly, [Trix (RGM 792.000)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trix_(dinosaur) "Trix (dinosaur)") is estimated to have been at least 30 years old at time of death.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-114)

Histology has also allowed the age of other specimens to be determined. Growth curves can be developed when the ages of different specimens are plotted on a graph along with their mass. A _T. rex_ growth curve is S-shaped, with juveniles remaining under 1,800 kg (4,000 lb) until approximately 14 years of age, when body size began to increase dramatically. During this rapid growth phase, a young _T. rex_ would gain an average of 600 kg (1,300 lb) a year for the next four years. At 18 years of age, the curve plateaus again, indicating that growth slowed dramatically. For example, only 600 kg (1,300 lb) separated the 28-year-old Sue from a 22-year-old Canadian specimen ([RTMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Tyrrell_Museum_of_Palaeontology "Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology") 81.12.1).[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-ericksonetal2004-41) A 2004 histological study performed by different workers corroborates these results, finding that rapid growth began to slow at around 16 years of age.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-hornerpadian2004-115)

_**Tyrannosaurus**_ ([/t ɪ ˌ r æ n ə ˈ s ɔː r ə s,t aɪ-/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"))[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-title-1) is a [genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genus "Genus") of large [theropod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theropoda "Theropoda") dinosaur. The [type species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_species "Type species")_**Tyrannosaurus rex**_ (_rex_ meaning 'king' in [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin")), often shortened to _**T. rex**_ or colloquially **T-Rex**, is one of the best represented theropods. It lived throughout what is now western [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), on what was then an island continent known as [Laramidia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laramidia "Laramidia"). _Tyrannosaurus_ had a much wider range than other [tyrannosaurids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosauridae "Tyrannosauridae"). [Fossils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fossil "Fossil") are found in a variety of [geological formations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geological_formations "Geological formations") which have been [dated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geochronology "Geochronology") to the late [Maastrichtian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastrichtian "Maastrichtian") age of the late [Cretaceous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous "Cretaceous") period, 69 to 66[million years ago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mya_(unit) "Mya (unit)"), with isolated specimens possibly indicating an earlier origin in the middle [Campanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campanian "Campanian") age. It was one of the last known members of the tyrannosaurids and among the last non-[avian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird "Bird") dinosaurs to exist before the [Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous%E2%80%93Paleogene_extinction_event "Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event").

Like other tyrannosaurids, _Tyrannosaurus_ was a [bipedal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biped "Biped") carnivore with a massive skull balanced by a long, heavy tail. Relative to its large and powerful hind limbs, the forelimbs of _Tyrannosaurus_ were short but unusually powerful for their size, and they had two clawed digits. The most complete specimen measures 12.3–12.4 m (40–41 ft) in length, but according to most modern estimates, _Tyrannosaurus_ could have exceeded sizes of 13 m (43 ft) in length, 3.7–4 m (12–13 ft) in hip height, and 8.8 t (8.7 long tons; 9.7 short tons) in mass. Although some other theropods might have rivaled or exceeded _Tyrannosaurus_ in [size](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur_size "Dinosaur size"), it is still among the largest known land predators, with its estimated bite force being the largest among all terrestrial animals. By far the largest carnivore in its environment, _Tyrannosaurus rex_ was most likely an [apex predator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apex_predator "Apex predator"), preying upon [hadrosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrosaur "Hadrosaur"), juvenile armored herbivores like [ceratopsians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceratopsia "Ceratopsia") and [ankylosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankylosaur "Ankylosaur"), and possibly [sauropods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauropod "Sauropod"). The question of whether _Tyrannosaurus_ was an apex predator or a pure scavenger was among the longest debates in [paleontology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleontology "Paleontology"). Most paleontologists today accept that _Tyrannosaurus_ was a predator, and the idea of _Tyrannosaurus_ being primarily a scavenger has been discredited.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus#cite_note-2)

Some [specimens of _Tyrannosaurus rex_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specimens_of_Tyrannosaurus "Specimens of Tyrannosaurus") are nearly complete skeletons. [Soft tissue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_tissue "Soft tissue") and [proteins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein "Protein") have been reported in at least one of these specimens. The abundance of fossil material has allowed significant research into many aspects of the animal's biology, including its life history and [biomechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biomechanics "Biomechanics"). The feeding habits, [physiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology"), and potential speed of _Tyrannosaurus rex_ are a few subjects of debate. Its [taxonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxonomy_(biology) "Taxonomy (biology)") is also controversial. The Asian _[Tarbosaurus bataar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarbosaurus\_bataar "Tarbosaurus bataar")_ is very closely related to _Tyrannosaurus_ and has sometimes been seen as a species of this genus. Several North American tyrannosaurids have been [synonymized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synonym_(biology) "Synonym (biology)") with _Tyrannosaurus_, while some _Tyrannosaurus_ specimens have been proposed as distinct species. The validity of these species, such as the more recently discovered _**T. mcraeensis**_, is contentious.

_Tyrannosaurus_ has been one of the best-known dinosaurs since the early 20th century. Science writer [Riley Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riley_Black "Riley Black") has called it the "ultimate dinosaur". Its fossils have been a popular attraction in museums and it has appeared in media like _[Jurassic Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jurassic\_Park "Jurassic Park")_.
