Riabinin (1930b) described several fragments from the [Yuliangze Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuliangze_Formation "Yuliangze Formation") of [Heilongjiang, China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heilongjiang "Heilongjiang") as _Albertosaurus periculosus_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-27) In the first edition of _[The Dinosauria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dinosauria "The Dinosauria")_, Molnar et al. (1990) listed _A. periculosus_ as a provisional synonym of _Tarbosaurus bataar_, as followed by Holtz (2004) in the second edition.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-:0-28)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-holtz2004-12) Olshevsky, Ford, and Yamamoto (1995) tentatively referred _A. periculosus_ to _Tarbosaurus_, listing it as _Tarbosaurus_? _periculosus_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-olshevskyford1995-10) Alifanov and Bolotsky (2002) referred material from the neighboring [Urduchukan Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Udurchukan_Formation "Udurchukan Formation") of [Amur, Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amur_Oblast "Amur Oblast"), to this taxon, but Bolotsky (2015) later regarded _A. periculosus_ as a _[nomen dubium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomen\_dubium "Nomen dubium")_.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-30)

Zhai et al. (1978) listed material from the Subashi Formation as _Tyrannosaurus turpanensis_.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-31) Since the specific name "turpanensis" was published in a faunal list only and lacks a description, it is a [_nomen nudum_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomen_nudum "Nomen nudum") according to ICZN Article 13.1.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-32) Olshevsky (1991) listed T. "turpanensis" under the combination _Tarbosaurus_ "turpanensis."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-:1-33) Several fragments from the Subashi Formation described by Dong (1977) as _Tarbosaurus_ sp. may represent this taxon.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-dong1977-22)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-:3-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-35) As with _Albertosaurus periculosus_, Molnar et al. (1990) listed _T._ "turpanensis" as a provisional synonym of _Tarbosaurus bataar_ without comment, as did [Holtz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_R._Holtz_Jr. "Thomas R. Holtz Jr.") (2004).[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-:0-28)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-holtz2004-12)

Dong (1979) described five teeth (IVPP V4733) discovered in the [Quipa Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qiupa_Formation "Qiupa Formation") of [Henan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henan "Henan"), China as a new species, _Tyrannosaurus luanchuanensis_.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-:2-36) Olshevsky (1991) listed it as _Tarbosaurus luanchuanensis_, and later in 1995, with Ford and Yamamoto, as _Jenghizkhan luanchuanensis._[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-:1-33)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-olshevskyford1995-10) Holtz (2004) listed it as a provisional synonym of _Tarbosaurus bataar_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-holtz2004-12)

Along with _Albertosaurus periculosus_, _Tyrannosaurus luanchuanensis_, and _Tyrannosaurus_ "turpanensis," _[Chingkankousaurus fragilis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chingkankousaurus "Chingkankousaurus")_ was considered a provisional junior synonym of _Tarbosaurus bataar_ by Holtz (2004), but it has since been assessed as dubious by Brusatte et al. (2013).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-holtz2004-12)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-37)

Named in 1976 by [Sergei Kurzanov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Kurzanov "Sergei Kurzanov"), _[Alioramus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alioramus "Alioramus")_ is another genus of tyrannosaurid from slightly older sediments in Mongolia.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-kurzanov1976-38) Several analyses have concluded _Alioramus_ was quite closely related to _Tarbosaurus_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-hurumsabath2003-3)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-currieetal2003-13) It was described as an adult, but its long, low skull is characteristic of a juvenile tyrannosaurid. This led Currie to speculate that _Alioramus_ might represent a juvenile _Tarbosaurus_, but he noted that the much higher tooth count and row of crests on top of the snout suggested otherwise.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-currie2003-39)

### Additional specimens

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Additional specimens")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Tarbosaurus_specimen_MPC-D_100_7.jpg/250px-Tarbosaurus_specimen_MPC-D_100_7.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tarbosaurus_specimen_MPC-D_100_7.jpg)

Juvenile _Tarbosaurus_ specimen MPC-D 107/7

In 1979 Dong Zhiming described several dinosaur remains from the strata of South China, reporting teeth, a dorsal vertebra, and several fragmentary foot bones of a tyrannosaurid. He tentatively referred these to _Tarbosaurus_ sp. given some similarities in tooth morphology as well as the general geographic proximity to the Nemegt Formation.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-:2-36) In 1993 Tomasz Jerzykiewiczz examined the general outcrops from the [Bayan Mandahu Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayan_Mandahu_Formation "Bayan Mandahu Formation") of China. In this paper, he reported isolated tyrannosaurid premaxillary and maxillary teeth, which he assigned to _Tarbosaurus_ without anatomical comparisons.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-J1993-40) Lev A. Nessov in 1995 reported a partial femur from the [Bostobe Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bostobe_Formation "Bostobe Formation") of [Kazakhstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakhstan "Kazakhstan") and referred it as _Tarbosaurus_ sp. without any diagnosis.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-41)

In 2004, David B. Weishampel and team listed a dubious _Tarbosaurus_? sp. as a component of the known dinosaur taxa of the [Campanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campanian "Campanian")-aged [Djadokhta Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Djadokhta_Formation "Djadokhta Formation") without further ado.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-42) Despite this referral, scattered, and very sparse tyrannosaurid remains are occasionally found in the strata of the Djadokhta Formation of Mongolia and none of these remains have ever been diagnostically assigned to _Tarbosaurus_ or even _T. bataar_.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-43)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-J1993-40)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-45) In addition, the extreme conditions of the Djadokhta Formation suggest that the remains of tyrannosaurids and other large-bodied dinosaurs from this unit represent passing by taxa foreign to the region.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-46)

During a large fossil prospection led by the Hayashibara Museum of Natural Sciences-Mongolian Paleontological Center Joint Expedition, a juvenile tyrannosaurid was discovered in 2006 from the highly fossiliferous Bügiin Tsav locality where adult specimens of _Tarbosaurus_ have been recovered. The specimen was found preserving a partial skeleton with a fairly complete skull. In 2011 this juvenile was formally described and referred to _Tarbosaurus bataar_, cataloged as MPC-D 107/7 within the collections of the [Mongolian Paleontological Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolian_Paleontological_Center?action=edit&redlink=1 "Mongolian Paleontological Center (page does not exist)").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-tsuihiji2011-47)

### Poached specimens

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Poached specimens")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/U.S._ICE_return_Tarbosaurus_bataar_skeleton_to_Mongolia_2013.jpg/250px-U.S._ICE_return_Tarbosaurus_bataar_skeleton_to_Mongolia_2013.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:U.S._ICE_return_Tarbosaurus_bataar_skeleton_to_Mongolia_2013.jpg)

_Tarbosaurus_ fossils that were smuggled to the US, and subsequently returned to Mongolia, at [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City")

_Tarbosaurus_ fossils are only found around the [Gobi Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gobi_Desert "Gobi Desert") of [Mongolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongolia "Mongolia") and [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), both of which ban their export, though some specimens have been looted by private collectors.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-48) A $1 million smuggling deal was uncovered when suspicions were raised about a catalog put out by Heritage Auctions for an event in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") on May 20, 2012. By Mongolian law, any specimen found in the [Gobi Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gobi_Desert "Gobi Desert") was to rest at an appropriate Mongolian institution and there was little reasonable doubt that the _Tarbosaurus bataar_ advertised on the catalog was a stolen one. The president of Mongolia and many paleontologists raised objections to the sale, which led to a last-minute investigation that confirmed that it was a specimen that can only be found in the Gobi Desert, rightfully belonging to Mongolia.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-49) During the court case ([United States v. One _Tyrannosaurus Bataar_ Skeleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._One_Tyrannosaurus_Bataar_Skeleton "United States v. One Tyrannosaurus Bataar Skeleton")), [Eric Prokopi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Prokopi "Eric Prokopi"), the smuggler, pleaded guilty to illegal smuggling and the dinosaur was returned to Mongolia in 2013, where it is temporarily displayed on [Sukhbaatar Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhbaatar_Square "Sukhbaatar Square"), the center of the city of [Ulaanbaatar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulaanbaatar "Ulaanbaatar").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-50) Prokopi had sold the dinosaur with a partner and fellow commercial hunter in England named Christopher Moore.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-51) The case led to the repatriation of dozens of Mongolian dinosaurs, including several skeletons of _Tarbosaurus bataar_.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-52)

### Skin impressions and footprints

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Skin impressions and footprints")]

Skin impressions were recovered from a large skeleton at the Bugiin Tsav locality that was subsequently destroyed by poachers. These impressions show non-overlapping scales with an average diameter of 2.4 millimeters (0.094 in) and pertain to the thoracic region of the individual, although the exact position can no longer be assessed due to the destruction of the skeleton.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-currie_03-53)

[Phil Currie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Currie "Phil Currie") and colleagues (2003) described two footprints from the Nemegt locality that probably pertain to _Tarbosaurus_. These tracks represent natural casts, which means that only the sandy infill of the tracks, not the tracks themselves, are preserved. The better-preserved track features skin impressions over large areas on and behind the toe impressions that are similar to those discovered in Bugiin Tsav. It also features vertical parallel slide marks that were left by scales when the foot was pushed into the ground. The track measures 61 centimeters (24 in) in length, thus representing a large individual. The second track, although even larger, was affected by [erosion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erosion "Erosion") and does not show any detail.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-currie_03-53)

In 1997, Ken Carpenter reported a damaged _Tarbosaurus_ skull with impressions of a dewlap or throat pouch beneath the lower jaws, based on a personal communication from Konstantin Mikhailov.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-54) Carpenter speculated that the pouch may have been used for display,  possibly being brightly colored and inflatable like a [frigatebird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frigatebird "Frigatebird")'s.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-55) In a 2019 communication to Mickey Mortimer, Mikhailov confirmed that this specimen had not been collected because it was on a heavy stone slab. He revealed that it had been discovered by [Sergei Kurzanov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Kurzanov "Sergei Kurzanov") and that it was Kurzanov himself who had originally interpreted the impressions as a throat structure.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-56) This specimen may be the same as one that was purportedly destroyed by poachers in 1992.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-57)

## Description

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Description")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Tarboscale.svg/250px-Tarboscale.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tarboscale.svg)

Size comparison of specimens representing various growth stages

Although slightly smaller than _Tyrannosaurus_, _Tarbosaurus_ was one of the largest [tyrannosaurines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurinae "Tyrannosaurinae"), with the type specimen PIN 551–1 measuring approximately 10 metres (33 ft) long, 3 metres (9.8 ft) tall at the hips, and weighing up to 4.5–5 metric tons (5.0–5.5 short tons).[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-58)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-:3-34)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-59) Some adult specimens have been estimated at more than 12 metres (39 ft) long.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-60) Other adult specimens were smaller, as MPC-D 107/2, ZPAL.MgD-I/4 and PIN 552-1 likely weighed around 2.2 metric tons (2.4 short tons) to 3.4 metric tons (3.7 short tons).[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-62) The largest known _Tarbosaurus_ skull is about 1.35 m (4.4 ft) long,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-63) which is larger than that of all other tyrannosaurids, aside from _Tyrannosaurus_.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-holtz2004-12)

### Skull

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Skull")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Tarbosaurus_labelled_skull.png/250px-Tarbosaurus_labelled_skull.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tarbosaurus_labelled_skull.png)

Labelled skull diagram of specimen ZPAL MgD−I/4

The skull was tall, like that of _Tyrannosaurus_, but not as wide, especially towards the rear. The unexpanded rear of the skull meant that _Tarbosaurus_' eyes did not face directly forwards, suggesting that it lacked the [binocular vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binocular_vision "Binocular vision") of _Tyrannosaurus_. Large [fenestrae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenestra_(anatomy) "Fenestra (anatomy)") in the skull reduced its overall weight and served as attachment points for muscles. Between 58 and 64 teeth lined its jaws. This tooth count is slightly more than that of _Tyrannosaurus_, but fewer than in smaller tyrannosaurids, like _[Gorgosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorgosaurus "Gorgosaurus")_ and _Alioramus_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-hurumsabath2003-3)

Most of its teeth were ovular in [cross section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_section_(geometry) "Cross section (geometry)"), although the teeth of the [premaxilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premaxilla "Premaxilla") at the tip of the upper jaw had a _D_-shaped cross section. However, this [heterodonty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heterodonty "Heterodonty") is characteristic of the family. The longest teeth were in the [maxilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxilla "Maxilla") (upper jaw bone), with [crowns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_(tooth_part) "Crown (tooth part)") up to 11.2 centimeters (4.4 in) long.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-maleev1974-7) In the [lower jaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandible "Mandible"), a ridge on the outer surface of the [angular bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_bone "Angular bone") articulated with the rear of the [dentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dentary "Dentary") bone, creating a locking mechanism unique to _Tarbosaurus_ and _Alioramus_. Other tyrannosaurids lacked this ridge and had more flexibility in the lower jaw.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-hurumsabath2003-3)

### Postcranial skeleton

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Postcranial skeleton")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/05/Tarbosaurus_skeletal.png/250px-Tarbosaurus_skeletal.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tarbosaurus_skeletal.png)

Skeletal reconstruction (ZPAL MgD I/4)

[![Image 17: Life restoration of the tyrannosaurid Tarbosaurus baatar](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8b/Tarbosaurus_baatar_paleoart_%282024%29.png/250px-Tarbosaurus_baatar_paleoart_%282024%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tarbosaurus_baatar_paleoart_(2024).png)

[Life restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleoart "Paleoart")

[Tyrannosaurids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosauridae "Tyrannosauridae") varied little in overall body form and _Tarbosaurus_ was no exception. The head was supported by an _S_-shaped neck, while the rest of the [vertebral column](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebral_column "Vertebral column"), including the tail, was held horizontally. _Tarbosaurus_ had tiny arms, proportionably to body size the smallest of all members in the family. The hands had two clawed digits each, with an additional unclawed third metacarpal found in some specimens, similar to those of closely related genera. Holtz has suggested that _Tarbosaurus_ also has a theropod reduction of fingers IV-I "developed further" than in other tyrannosaurids,[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-Holtz_in_Carpenter2001-64) as the second metacarpal in the _Tarbosaurus_ specimens he studied is less than twice the length of the first metacarpal. Other tyrannosaurids have a second metacarpal about twice the length of the first metacarpal. Also, the third metacarpal in _Tarbosaurus_ is proportionally shorter than in other tyrannosaurids. In other tyrannosaurids, like _[Albertosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albertosaurus "Albertosaurus")_ and _[Daspletosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daspletosaurus "Daspletosaurus")_, the third metacarpal is often longer than the first metacarpal, while in the _Tarbosaurus_ specimens studied by Holtz, the third metacarpal is shorter than the first.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-holtz2004-12) In contrast to the arms, the three-toed legs were long, thick, and muscular to support the body in a bipedal posture. The long, heavy tail served as a [counterweight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterweight "Counterweight") to the head and torso, while also placing the [center of gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_of_gravity "Center of gravity") directly over the hips.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-maleev1955b-5)

## Classification

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Classification")]

_Tarbosaurus_ is classified as a [theropod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theropod "Theropod") in the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae of the family [Tyrannosauridae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosauridae "Tyrannosauridae"). Other members include _Tyrannosaurus_ and the earlier _[Daspletosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daspletosaurus "Daspletosaurus")_, both from North America,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-carretal2005-15) and possibly the Mongolian genus _Alioramus_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-hurumsabath2003-3)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-currieetal2003-13) Animals in this subfamily are more closely related to _Tyrannosaurus_ than to _[Albertosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albertosaurus "Albertosaurus")_ and are known for their robust build with proportionally larger skulls and longer [femurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femur "Femur") than in the other subfamily, Albertosaurinae.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-holtz2004-12)

_Tarbosaurus bataar_ was originally described as a species of _Tyrannosaurus_,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-maleev1955a-2) an arrangement that has been supported by some more recent studies.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-carretal2005-15)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-carpenter1992-9) Others prefer to keep the genera separate, while still recognizing them as [sister taxa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sister_taxa "Sister taxa").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-holtz2004-12) A 2003 [cladistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cladistic "Cladistic") analysis based on skull features instead identified _Alioramus_ as the closest known relative of _Tarbosaurus_, as the two genera share skull characteristics that are related to stress distribution and are not found in other tyrannosaurines. If proven, this relationship would argue against _Tarbosaurus_ being a synonym of _Tyrannosaurus_ and would suggest that separate tyrannosaurine lineages [evolved convergently](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergent_evolution "Convergent evolution") in Asia and North America.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-hurumsabath2003-3)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-currieetal2003-13) The two known specimens of _Alioramus_, which show juvenile characteristics, are not likely juvenile individuals of _Tarbosaurus_ because of their much higher tooth count (76 to 78 teeth) and their unique row of bony bumps along the top of their snouts.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-currie2003-39)

The discovery of _[Lythronax argestes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lythronax\_argestes "Lythronax argestes")_, a much earlier tyrannosaurine, further reveals the close relationship between _Tyrannosaurus_ and _Tarbosaurus_. It was also discovered that _Lythronax_ is a sister taxon to a clade consisting of [Campanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campanian "Campanian") genus _Zhuchengtyrannus_, and the [Maastrichtian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastrichtian "Maastrichtian") genera _Tyrannosaurus_ and _Tarbosaurus_. Further studies of _Lythronax_ also suggest that the Asian [tyrannosauroids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosauroidea "Tyrannosauroidea") were part of one evolutionary radiation.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-65)

## Paleobiology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Paleobiology")]

### Ontogeny

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Ontogeny")]

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Tarbosaurus_adult_%26_juvenile_skulls.png/250px-Tarbosaurus_adult_%26_juvenile_skulls.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tarbosaurus_adult_&_juvenile_skulls.png)

Skull of juvenile (top, MPC-D 107/7), and adult (bottom, ZPAL MgD I/4)

Most specimens of _Tarbosaurus_ represent adult or subadult individuals, while juveniles remain very rare. Nevertheless, the 2006 discovery of a juvenile individual (MPC-D 107/7) with a complete, 290-millimeter (0.95 ft) long skull was reported and described in 2011, providing information on the life history of this dinosaur. This individual was probably 2 to 3 years old at the time of death. Compared to adult skulls, the juvenile skull was weakly constructed and the teeth were thin, indicating different food preferences in juveniles and adults that reduced competition between different age groups. Examination of the sclerotic rings in this juvenile _Tarbosaurus_ suggests they may also have been crepuscular or nocturnal hunters. Whether or not the adult _Tarbosaurus_ were also nocturnal is currently unknown due to the lack of fossil evidence to suggest so.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-tsuihiji2011-47) Ontogenetic changes identified in the [frontal bones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontal_bone "Frontal bone") suggests that the allometric growth of _Tarbosaurus_ was similar to that of North American tyrannosaurids.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-67)

### Senses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Senses")]

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Tarbosaurus_and_Iguanodon_Braincase.jpg/250px-Tarbosaurus_and_Iguanodon_Braincase.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tarbosaurus_and_Iguanodon_Braincase.jpg)

Braincase of _Tarbosaurus_ (left) next to the braincaise of _[Iguanodon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iguanodon "Iguanodon")_ (right)

A _Tarbosaurus_ skull found in 1948 by Soviet and Mongolian scientists (PIN 553–1, originally called _Gorgosaurus lancinator_) included the skull cavity that held the brain. Making a plaster [cast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casting "Casting"), called an _[endocast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endocranial\_cast "Endocranial cast")_, of the inside of this cavity allowed Maleev to make preliminary observations about the shape of a _Tarbosaurus_ brain.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-maleev1965-68) A newer [polyurethane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyurethane "Polyurethane") rubber cast allowed a more detailed study of _Tarbosaurus_ brain structure and function.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-savelievalifanov2005-69)

The endocranial structure of _Tarbosaurus_ was similar to that of _Tyrannosaurus_,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-brochu2000-70) differing only in the positions of some [cranial nerve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cranial_nerve "Cranial nerve") roots, including the [trigeminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigeminal_nerve "Trigeminal nerve") and [accessory nerves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessory_nerve "Accessory nerve"). Tyrannosaurid brains were more similar to those of [crocodilians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodilia "Crocodilia") and other nonavian reptiles than they were to [birds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird "Bird"). The total brain volume for a 12 meters (39 ft) long _Tarbosaurus_ is estimated at only 184 cubic centimeters (11.2 cu in).[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-savelievalifanov2005-69)

The large size of the [olfactory bulbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olfactory_bulb "Olfactory bulb"), as well as the [terminal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_nerve "Terminal nerve") and [olfactory nerves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olfactory_nerve "Olfactory nerve"), suggest that _Tarbosaurus_ had a highly keen [sense of smell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sense_of_smell "Sense of smell"), as was also the case with _Tyrannosaurus_. The [vomeronasal bulb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olfactory_bulb#Accessory_olfactory_bulb "Olfactory bulb") is large and differentiated from the olfactory bulb, which was initially suggested as being indicative of a well-developed [Jacobsen's organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vomeronasal_organ "Vomeronasal organ"), which was used to detect [pheromones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheromone "Pheromone"). This may imply that _Tarbosaurus_ had complex mating behavior.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-savelievalifanov2005-69) However, the identification of the vomeronasal bulb has been challenged by other researchers because they are not present in any living archosaurs.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-alio-71)

The [auditory nerve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auditory_nerve "Auditory nerve") was also large, suggesting good [hearing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearing_(sense) "Hearing (sense)"), which may have been useful for auditory [communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_communication "Animal communication") and spatial awareness. The nerve had a well-developed [vestibular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestibular_system "Vestibular system") component as well, which implies a good sense of balance and coordination. In contrast, the nerves and brain structures associated with [eyesight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyesight "Eyesight") were smaller and undeveloped. The [midbrain tectum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midbrain_tectum "Midbrain tectum"), responsible for visual processing in reptiles, was very small in _Tarbosaurus_, as were the [optic nerve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optic_nerve "Optic nerve") and the [oculomotor nerve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oculomotor_nerve "Oculomotor nerve"), which controls eye movement. Unlike _Tyrannosaurus_, which had forward-facing eyes that provided accurate binocular vision, _Tarbosaurus_ had a narrower skull more typical of other tyrannosaurids in which the eyes faced primarily sideways. All of this suggests that _Tarbosaurus_ relied more on its senses of smell and hearing than on its eyesight.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-savelievalifanov2005-69) It has been suggested that the lack of binocular vision in Asian tyrannosaurs, like _Tarbosaurus_, might have been correlated with a greater amount of scavenging resources provided by sauropod carcasses, which might have afforded them a less active predatory lifestyle when compared to the North American forms, meaning they would need less predatory adaptations.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-72) However, this is contradicted by numerous lines of evidence indicating _Tarbosaurus_ was actively preying on hadrosaurs, titanosaur sauropods, and other large bodied herbivores in its ecosystem.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-sciencedirect.com-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-academia.edu-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-Tumanova-76)

### Skull mechanics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Skull mechanics")]

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Tarbosaurus_MPC-D_100_60_skull_%28front%29.jpg/120px-Tarbosaurus_MPC-D_100_60_skull_%28front%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tarbosaurus_MPC-D_100_60_skull_(front).jpg)

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/Tarbosaurus_MPC-D_100_60_skull_%283%29.jpg/250px-Tarbosaurus_MPC-D_100_60_skull_%283%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tarbosaurus_MPC-D_100_60_skull_(3).jpg)

Skull from the front and right

The skull of _Tarbosaurus_ was completely described for the first time in 2003. Scientists noted key differences between _Tarbosaurus_ and the North American tyrannosaurids. Many of these differences are related to the handling of stress by the skull bones during a bite. When the upper jaw bit down on an object, [force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Force "Force") was transmitted up through the maxilla, the primary tooth-bearing bone of the upper jaw, into surrounding skull bones. In North American tyrannosaurids, this force went from the maxilla into the fused [nasal bones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_bone "Nasal bone") on top of the snout, which were firmly connected in the rear to the [lacrimal bones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacrimal_bone "Lacrimal bone") by bony struts. These struts locked the two bones together, suggesting that force was then transmitted from the nasals to the lacrimals.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-hurumsabath2003-3)

_Tarbosaurus_ lacked these bony struts and the connection between the nasals and lacrimals was weak. Instead, a backwards projection of the maxilla was massively developed in _Tarbosaurus_ and fit inside a sheath formed from the lacrimal. This projection was a thin, bony plate in North American tyrannosaurids. The large backwards projection suggests that force was transmitted more directly from the maxilla to the lacrimal in _Tarbosaurus_. The lacrimal was also more firmly anchored to the [frontal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontal_bone "Frontal bone") and [prefrontal bones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefrontal_bone "Prefrontal bone") in _Tarbosaurus_. The well-developed connections between the [maxilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxilla "Maxilla"), [lacrimal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacrimal_bone "Lacrimal bone"), [frontal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontal_bone "Frontal bone"), and [prefrontal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefrontal_bone "Prefrontal bone") would have made its entire upper jaw much more rigid.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-hurumsabath2003-3)

Another major difference between _Tarbosaurus_ and its North American relatives was its more rigid mandible. While many theropods, including North American tyrannosaurids, had some degree of flexibility between the bones in the rear of the mandible and the dentary in the front, _Tarbosaurus_ had a locking mechanism formed from a ridge on the surface of the angular, which articulated with a square process on the rear of the dentary.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-hurumsabath2003-3)

Some scientists have [hypothesized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypothesis "Hypothesis") that the more rigid skull of _Tarbosaurus_ was an adaptation to hunting the massive [titanosaurid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanosaurid "Titanosaurid")[sauropods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauropod "Sauropod") found in the Nemegt Formation, which did not exist in most of North America during the Late Cretaceous. The differences in skull mechanics also affect tyrannosaurid phylogeny. _Tarbosaurus_-like articulations between the skull bones are also seen in _Alioramus_ from Mongolia, suggesting that it is the closest relative of _Tarbosaurus_. Similarities between _Tarbosaurus_ and _Tyrannosaurus_ might therefore be related to their large size, independently developed through [convergent evolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convergent_evolution "Convergent evolution").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-hurumsabath2003-3)

### Bite force and feeding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Bite force and feeding")]

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Saurolophus_MPC-D_100_764_humerus_injuries.png/250px-Saurolophus_MPC-D_100_764_humerus_injuries.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Saurolophus_MPC-D_100_764_humerus_injuries.png)

Left humerus of _S. angustirostris_ MPC-D 100/764, showing multiple bite marks attributed to _Tarbosaurus_

In 2001, [Bruce Rothschild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Rothschild?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bruce Rothschild (page does not exist)") and others published a study examining evidence for [stress fractures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress_fracture "Stress fracture") and [tendon avulsions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avulsion_fracture "Avulsion fracture") in [theropod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theropoda "Theropoda") dinosaurs and the implications for their behavior. Since stress fractures are caused by repeated trauma rather than singular events, they are more likely to be caused by regular behavior than other types of injuries. None of the eighteen _Tarbosaurus_ foot bones examined in the study were found to have a stress fracture, but one of the ten examined hand bones was found to have one. Stress fractures in the hands have special behavioral significance compared to those found in the feet, since stress fractures there can be obtained while running or during migration. Hand injuries, by contrast, are more likely to be obtained while in contact with struggling prey. The presence of stress fractures and tendon avulsions, in general, provide evidence for a "very active" predation-based diet instead of obligate scavenging.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-rothschild-dino-77)

As for its bite force, it was revealed in 2005 that _Tarbosaurus_ had a bite force of around 8,000 to 10,000 pounds per square inch of force, meaning that it could crush bones just like its North American relative, _Tyrannosaurus_.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-78)

David W. E. Hone and Mahito Watabe in 2011 reported the left humerus of a nearly complete _[Saurolophus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saurolophus "Saurolophus")_ skeleton (MPC-D 100/764) from the Bügiin Tsav locality of the Nemegt Formation, which was [heavily damaged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleopathology "Paleopathology") from bite marks attributed to _Tarbosaurus_. As suggested by the lack of damage to the rest of the skeleton (such as large wounds in skeletal remains indicative of [predation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predation "Predation")), this tyrannosaurid was likely [scavenging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scavenging "Scavenging") an already dead _Saurolophus_. It is unlikely that a large-bodied predator, such as _Tarbosaurus_, would have left sparse feeding traces on a single humerus when having an entire carcass to feed on. The humerus shows three distinctive feeding methods, interpreted as punctures, drag marks, and bite−and−drag marks. Hone and Watabe noted that bite marks were mostly located at the deltopectoral crest, suggesting that this _Tarbosaurus_ was actively selecting which biting style to employ so it could scavenge the bone.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-79)

[![Image 35](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Tarbosaurus_teeth.jpg/250px-Tarbosaurus_teeth.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tarbosaurus_teeth.jpg)

Teeth of specimen MPC-D 100/6 featuring serrations

In 2012, bite marks on two fragmentary [gastralia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastralium "Gastralium") of the holotype specimen of the large [ornithomimosaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornithomimosauria "Ornithomimosauria")_[Deinocheirus mirificus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinocheirus "Deinocheirus")_ were reported. The size and shape of the bite marks match the teeth of _Tarbosaurus_, the largest known predator from the [Nemegt Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nemegt_Formation "Nemegt Formation"). Various types of feeding traces were identified. These include punctures, gouges, striae, fragmentary teeth, and combinations of the above marks. The bite marks probably represent feeding behavior instead of aggression between the species and the fact that bite marks were not found elsewhere on the body indicates the predator focused on internal organs. _Tarbosaurus_ bite marks have also been identified on hadrosaur and sauropod fossils, but theropod bite marks on bones of other theropods are very rare in the fossil record.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-academia.edu-74) In addition, a wound found on a _Tarchia_ skull may have been inflicted by a _Tarbosaurus_. The ankylosaur would have survived the attack but eventually succumbed to a pathology in the healing process.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-Tumanova-76)

A 2020 study involving stable isotopes found that _Tarbosaurus_ primarily hunted large dinosaurs in its environment, most notably [titanosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titanosauria "Titanosauria") and [hadrosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrosauridae "Hadrosauridae").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-sciencedirect.com-73)

## Paleoenvironment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Paleoenvironment")]

### Nemegt Formation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Nemegt Formation")]

[![Image 36](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Cretaceous-aged_dinosaur_fossil_localities_of_Mongolia.PNG/250px-Cretaceous-aged_dinosaur_fossil_localities_of_Mongolia.PNG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cretaceous-aged_dinosaur_fossil_localities_of_Mongolia.PNG)

[Cretaceous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous "Cretaceous")-aged dinosaur fossil localities of Mongolia; _Tarbosaurus_ was collected in area A (left).

The vast majority of known _Tarbosaurus_ fossils were recovered from the [Nemegt Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nemegt_Formation "Nemegt Formation") in the [Gobi Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gobi_Desert "Gobi Desert") of southern Mongolia.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-jerzykiewiczrussell1991-80)[U-Pb dating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U-Pb_dating "U-Pb dating") from teeth of _Tarbosaurus_ suggested that the deposition of the middle Nemegt Formation happened before 66.7 ± 2.5 Ma, during the [Maastrichtian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastrichtian "Maastrichtian") age of the Late Cretaceous, though whether the depositional age of the formation dates back to the late [Campanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campanian "Campanian") remains unresolved.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-TanabeMyu-1)

_Tarbosaurus_ is found chiefly in the Nemegt Formation, whose sediments preserve large river channels and soil deposits that indicate a far more humid climate than those suggested by the underlying [Barun Goyot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barun_Goyot_Formation "Barun Goyot Formation") and [Djadochta Formations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Djadochta_Formation "Djadochta Formation"). However, [caliche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliche_(mineral) "Caliche (mineral)") deposits indicate at least periodic droughts. Sediment was deposited in the channels and floodplains of large rivers. The rock [facies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facies "Facies") of this formation suggest the presence of mudflats and shallow lakes. Sediments also indicate that there existed a rich habitat, offering diverse food in abundant amounts that could sustain massive [Cretaceous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous "Cretaceous") dinosaurs.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-81)

The area would have been semi-arid during certain times of the year.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-sciencedirect.com-73) The environment was likely dominated by [Araucarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Araucariaceae "Araucariaceae") conifer forests,[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-sciencedirect.com-73) which also contained [ginkgos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginkgo "Ginkgo"), reed grasses, [fagalean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagales "Fagales") trees, cycad-like plants, [sycamores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platanus "Platanus") (plane trees), [bald cypresses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxodium "Taxodium"), katsura relatives, [pondweeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pondweed "Pondweed"), tupelos, duckweeds, lotuses, and sedges.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-82)

Restorations of _Tarbosaurus_ in the paleoenvironments of the Nemegt Formation along with contemporary paleofauna

Occasional [mollusk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusk "Mollusk") fossils are found, as well as a variety of other aquatic animals, such as fish and turtles.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-jerzykiewiczrussell1991-80) Crocodilians included several species of _[Paralligator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paralligator "Paralligator")_, a genus with teeth adapted for crushing shells.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-efimov1983-83)[Mammal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal "Mammal") fossils are exceedingly rare in the Nemegt Formation, but many birds have been found, including the [enantiornithine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enantiornithine "Enantiornithine")_[Gurilynia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurilynia "Gurilynia")_ and the [hesperornithiform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hesperornithes "Hesperornithes")_[Judinornis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judinornis "Judinornis")_, as well as _[Teviornis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teviornis "Teviornis")_, an early representative of the still-existing [Anseriformes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anseriformes "Anseriformes"). Scientists have described many dinosaurs from the Nemegt Formation, including the [ankylosaurids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankylosaurids "Ankylosaurids")_[Tarchia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarchia "Tarchia")_ and _[Saichania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saichania "Saichania")_ and the [pachycephalosaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pachycephalosaur "Pachycephalosaur")_[Prenocephale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prenocephale "Prenocephale")_.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-jerzykiewiczrussell1991-80)

By far the largest predator known from the formation, adult _Tarbosaurus_ most likely preyed upon large hadrosaurs, such as _[Saurolophus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saurolophus "Saurolophus")_ and _[Barsboldia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barsboldia "Barsboldia")_, or sauropods, such as _[Nemegtosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nemegtosaurus "Nemegtosaurus")_ and _[Opisthocoelicaudia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opisthocoelicaudia "Opisthocoelicaudia")_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-hurumsabath2003-3) Adults would have received little competition from small theropods, such as the small [tyrannosaurid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurid "Tyrannosaurid")_[Alioramus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alioramus "Alioramus")_, [troodontids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troodontid "Troodontid") (_[Borogovia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borogovia "Borogovia")_, _[Tochisaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tochisaurus "Tochisaurus")_, _[Zanabazar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zanabazar\_(dinosaur) "Zanabazar (dinosaur)")_), [oviraptorosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oviraptorosaur "Oviraptorosaur") (_[Elmisaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elmisaurus "Elmisaurus")_, _[Nemegtomaia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nemegtomaia "Nemegtomaia")_, _[Rinchenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rinchenia "Rinchenia")_) or _[Bagaraatan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagaraatan "Bagaraatan")_, sometimes considered a [basal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basal_(phylogenetics) "Basal (phylogenetics)")[tyrannosauroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosauroid "Tyrannosauroid"). Other theropods, like the gigantic _[Therizinosaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Therizinosaurus "Therizinosaurus")_, might have been [herbivorous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbivore "Herbivore") and [ornithomimosaurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornithomimosaur "Ornithomimosaur"), such as _[Anserimimus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anserimimus "Anserimimus")_, _[Gallimimus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallimimus "Gallimimus")_, and gigantic _[Deinocheirus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deinocheirus "Deinocheirus")_ might have been omnivores that only took small prey and were therefore no competition for _Tarbosaurus_. However, as in other large tyrannosaurids, as well as modern [Komodo dragons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komodo_dragon "Komodo dragon"), juveniles and subadult _Tarbosaurus_ would have filled niches between the massive adults and these smaller theropods.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-holtz2004-12)

### Subashi Formation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tarbosaurus&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Subashi Formation")]

The [Subashi Formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subashi_Formation "Subashi Formation"), in which _Shanshanosaurus_ remains were discovered, dates to both the [Campanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campanian "Campanian") and [Maastrichtian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastrichtian "Maastrichtian") stages.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-shenmateer1992-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyrannosaurus_luanchuanensis#cite_note-85)
